Lyndon B. Johnson. The thirty-sixth president of the United States, serving from 1963 to 1969. Ascending to the presidency following John F. Kennedy's assassination, LBJ was a Texas Democrat and master legislator who championed the Great Society, an ambitious agenda of civil rights reform, anti-poverty programs, and federal aid to education.

Johnson became president unexpectedly at age fifty-five following Kennedy's assassination on November 22, 1963. He quickly moved to consolidate power and promote Kennedy's stalled legislation. He orchestrated passage of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which banned racial discrimination in public accommodations, and won the 1964 election in a landslide over Republican Barry Goldwater.

He introduced the Great Society program, which included Medicare, Medicaid, federal aid to education through the Elementary and Secondary Education Act, the Head Start program, and the War on Poverty. Yet his presidency came to be consumed and ultimately defined by the Vietnam War. He escalated American military involvement dramatically from about nine hundred advisors when he took office to over five hundred thirty-six thousand troops by 1968, following the Gulf of Tonkin incident in 1964.

He pushed through the Voting Rights Act of 1965, landmark legislation that empowered federal oversight of elections in states with histories of racial discrimination. On March 31, 1968, during a televised address, Johnson announced he would not seek reelection, citing the divisiveness of the war. He left office with his approval rating deeply damaged by the Vietnam conflict that had come to overshadow his historic domestic achievements.
